subtype: Approach: trust the output because it sounds fluent [Pitfall]
passage:
Note on Aditi's quarterly report, written by Reena, team manager.

On Tuesday I was checking Aditi's draft before it went to the client and noticed a growth figure that looked too neat. I searched for its source and found nothing. When I asked, Aditi said the tool had produced it and it sounded right, so she added it without checking.

The number was invented. Had it gone out, we would have lost credibility with the client.

I sat with Aditi and we removed the figure, replaced it with the real number from the records, and re-sent the draft. She was upset and apologised twice. I told her that fluent writing is not proof of accuracy, and we agreed that every figure gets a source line before I see it.

qa.q: On which day did Reena notice the figure?
What might Aditi have been feeling when she apologised twice?
qa.a: Aditi was upset and embarrassed, realising the invented number could have harmed the client's trust.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to catch such problems herself, and why?
qa.a: Aditi could add a source line for every figure and check each against the records before sharing, because a fluent answer proves nothing about accuracy.

qa.q: What would have changed for the client if the figure had gone out?
qa.a: The client would have trusted a number that was not real, and the team would have lost credibility once it was discovered.

grounding: A young analyst uses a tool-generated figure without checking, and the manager finds the number invented, mistaking fluency for accuracy.

passage:
Thursday night.
Today was bad. Yash called me into the small meeting room at four and put my market report on the table with one number circled in red: "62 percent of small shops plan to go online this year."
"Where's this from?" he asked.
I said the tool gave it. It wrote the whole paragraph so smoothly, with a survey name and everything, that I didn't think to check. Yash had searched for the survey. It doesn't exist. Nobody has that number.
The report had already gone to the client's team this morning. Yash has to send a correction tomorrow with his name on it. He wasn't loud, which somehow made it worse. He just said, "Sounding right isn't the same as being right, Vinita."
I keep thinking about every other smooth paragraph I've trusted.

qa.q: What number was circled in red on the report?
qa.a: 62 percent of small shops plan to go online this year.

qa.q: How does Vinita feel writing this entry?
qa.a: Vinita feels ashamed and shaken, and is now uneasy about every other smooth paragraph trusted before.

qa.q: What would you change first in Vinita's process, and why?
qa.a: Every figure should be traced to a real source before it goes in a report, because a fluent paragraph can invent a survey that does not exist.

qa.q: How is Yash affected by the mistake?
qa.a: Yash has to send a correction to the client with his own name on it, so the mistake costs his credibility too.

grounding: Shows a young analyst trusting a fluent tool-generated figure, which the manager finds to be invented, harming credibility.
